questions.passage: When chief engineer Washington Roebling became seriously ill in the 1870s, his wife, Emily Warren Roebling, taught herself higher mathematics and engineering principles and ______blank much of the day-to-day work of building the Brooklyn Bridge, relaying instructions to workers and answering officials' technical questions.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The text says that Emily Warren Roebling relayed instructions to workers and answered officials' technical questions, which describes someone directing the project's daily work. "Oversaw" fits that context. "Prevented" and "postponed" contradict the text, which describes the work moving forward, and "imagined" suggests the work existed only in her mind.

questions.passage: Because Venus is covered by thick clouds that reflect most of the sunlight striking them, the planet's surface cannot be ______blank directly by telescopes that rely on visible light. Instead, scientists have mapped Venus's surface using radar, which can penetrate the clouds.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Because Venus's clouds reflect visible light, telescopes that rely on visible light can't see the surface, which is why scientists use radar instead. "Observed" (seen) fits. Telescopes don't heat, alter, or shield a planet's surface, so the other choices don't make sense.

questions.passage: Although critics initially dismissed the loose brushwork of Impressionist painters as unfinished, many later scholars came to see that apparent roughness as ______blank: artists such as Berthe Morisot carefully cultivated quick, visible strokes in order to capture the shifting effects of light.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The colon introduces an explanation: Morisot "carefully cultivated" her quick, visible strokes. That makes the roughness "deliberate," or intentional. "Accidental" is the view the later scholars rejected. "Conventional" doesn't fit a style critics found strange, and nothing in the text suggests the roughness was "temporary."

questions.passage: Geologists once regarded fault creep, in which rocks on either side of a fault slide past each other gradually instead of locking and then releasing suddenly in an earthquake, as largely ______blank to seismic hazard assessment. Recent models complicate that view, suggesting that creeping segments can transfer stress to adjacent locked sections of a fault and thereby influence where large earthquakes begin.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The second sentence says recent models "complicate that view" by showing creeping segments can affect where large earthquakes begin. So the earlier view must have been that creep was of little importance to seismic hazard assessment, or "peripheral." "Indispensable" is the opposite of the older view. "Antithetical" (directly opposed) and "analogous" (similar) don't describe how relevant creep was thought to be.

questions.passage: In 1861, the completion of the first transcontinental telegraph line allowed messages to travel between the East and West Coasts of the United States in minutes. Just days later, the Pony Express, a mail service that had relied on relays of horseback riders to carry letters between Missouri and California in about ten days, announced that it would cease operations. Although the Pony Express lasted only about eighteen months, it remains one of the most famous ventures in the history of the American West.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It presents a claim that the rest of the text argues against.
It describes an immediate consequence of the development discussed in the first sentence.
It explains why the Pony Express was able to deliver mail so quickly.
It offers an example of the lasting fame mentioned in the final sentence.
questions.correct_answer: It describes an immediate consequence of the development discussed in the first sentence.
questions.explanation: The first sentence describes the transcontinental telegraph, which sent messages in minutes. The underlined sentence says that "just days later" the Pony Express, which took about ten days, announced it would shut down, which is a direct result of the faster telegraph. Nothing in the text argues against the sentence (A). It doesn't explain the Pony Express's speed (C), and it describes the service ending, not its fame (D).

questions.passage: For decades, astronomers assumed that the rings of Saturn formed along with the planet itself, roughly 4.5 billion years ago. Measurements made by NASA's Cassini spacecraft, however, indicated that the rings contain surprisingly little of the dark dust that constantly falls into the Saturn system from outside it. Because such dust should build up steadily over time, some researchers have argued that the rings' clean, icy appearance points to a much younger age, perhaps only a few hundred million years. Others counter that processes not yet understood might continually clean the rings, so the question of their age remains open.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It introduces a scientific mission, summarizes the data the mission gathered, and then explains why those data confirmed a traditional view.
It outlines two competing hypotheses, describes an experiment designed to test them, and then reports which hypothesis the experiment supported.
It explains how planetary rings form, compares Saturn's rings with those of other planets, and then predicts how Saturn's rings will change over time.
It describes a long-held assumption, presents evidence that has led some researchers to question that assumption, and then notes that a possible alternative explanation leaves the issue unresolved.
questions.correct_answer: It describes a long-held assumption, presents evidence that has led some researchers to question that assumption, and then notes that a possible alternative explanation leaves the issue unresolved.
questions.explanation: The text begins with what astronomers "for decades" assumed (the rings are as old as Saturn), then presents Cassini data on the rings' cleanliness that led some researchers to argue for a younger age, and ends with the counterargument that unknown cleaning processes could explain the data, so "the question remains open." A is wrong because the data challenged the traditional view. B is wrong because no experiment settles the question. C is wrong because the text doesn't explain ring formation, discuss other planets, or make a prediction.

questions.passage:
Text 1

When practical photography emerged in the mid-nineteenth century, it could record a scene with a precision no painter could match. According to many art historians, this development pushed painters away from exact representation and toward experiments with color, light, and brushwork, experiments that culminated in the rise of Impressionism in the 1870s.

Text 2

It is tempting to credit photography with inspiring painters' turn away from detailed realism, but the timing does not fully support this idea. In the early 1820s, English painter John Constable was already producing rapid, loosely brushed oil sketches of clouds that aimed to capture fleeting effects of weather and light, more than a decade before the first practical photographic processes were announced in 1839.
questions.question: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the art historians' view presented in Text 1?
options: By arguing that Impressionist painters were less interested in photography than earlier painters were
By agreeing that photography influenced painters but claiming that this influence began well before 1839
By suggesting that photography could not have been the only factor behind painters' interest in capturing fleeting effects, since such interest existed before practical photography did
By pointing out that Constable's cloud sketches were more precise than early photographs were
questions.correct_answer: By suggesting that photography could not have been the only factor behind painters' interest in capturing fleeting effects, since such interest existed before practical photography did
questions.explanation: Text 1 reports the view that photography pushed painters toward loose experiments with light. Text 2 says "the timing does not fully support this idea," noting that Constable was painting loose sketches of fleeting weather effects in the early 1820s, over a decade before photography existed in practical form. So the author of Text 2 would say photography can't fully explain the trend. Text 2 doesn't compare Impressionists' interest in photography (A), doesn't claim photography's influence predated photography (B), and doesn't call Constable's loose sketches more precise than photographs (D).

questions.passage: Many people imagine deserts as places where water plays almost no role, but water shapes desert landscapes dramatically. Because desert soils are often hard-packed and have little vegetation to absorb rainfall, a single heavy storm can send water rushing across the ground in a flash flood. Such floods can carve deep channels called arroyos, move large boulders, and deposit thick layers of sediment in just a few hours.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Deserts receive more rainfall each year than most people realize.
Although rain is infrequent in deserts, water can dramatically change desert landscapes.
Flash floods are more dangerous in deserts than they are in any other environment.
Arroyos are the most common type of landform found in deserts.
questions.correct_answer: Although rain is infrequent in deserts, water can dramatically change desert landscapes.
questions.explanation: The text opens by saying that although people imagine water plays little role in deserts, "water shapes desert landscapes dramatically," and the rest of the text explains how flash floods carve channels and move boulders and sediment. The text never says deserts get a lot of rain (A), compares flood danger across environments (C), or ranks landforms (D).

questions.passage: Digging beneath a river is dangerous because the soft, waterlogged ground can collapse. For the Thames Tunnel in London, completed in 1843, engineer Marc Isambard Brunel used a device called a tunnelling shield: a large iron frame divided into cells, in each of which a worker removed a small amount of earth at a time while the rest of the tunnel face stayed supported. As the shield was pushed forward, bricklayers immediately lined the newly exposed section of tunnel with brick.
questions.question: According to the text, how did the tunnelling shield help reduce the danger of digging beneath the river?
options: It drained water from the soft ground before any digging began.
It allowed workers to dig the tunnel from both riverbanks at the same time.
It eliminated the need to line the tunnel with brick.
It kept most of the tunnel face supported while workers removed earth a little at a time.
questions.correct_answer: It kept most of the tunnel face supported while workers removed earth a little at a time.
questions.explanation: The text says each worker removed "a small amount of earth at a time while the rest of the tunnel face stayed supported," which addresses the danger that soft ground would collapse. The text doesn't mention draining the ground (A) or digging from both banks (B). And bricklayers still lined the tunnel (C).

questions.passage:
The following text is from Jane Austen's 1813 novel Pride and Prejudice.

It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife. However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters.
questions.question: What does the text most strongly suggest about the families in the neighbourhood?
options: They are eager to learn a wealthy newcomer's true feelings before forming any opinions about him.
They believe that a wealthy single man's marriage should be decided by his own wishes.
They confidently form expectations about a wealthy newcomer that reflect their own hopes more than any knowledge of him.
They are suspicious of wealthy men who move into the neighbourhood without families.
questions.correct_answer: They confidently form expectations about a wealthy newcomer that reflect their own hopes more than any knowledge of him.
questions.explanation: The narrator says that however little is known of such a man's "feelings or views," the families are so sure he wants a wife that they consider him "the rightful property" of one of their daughters. Their certainty rests on their own interests, not on knowledge of him. A is wrong because the families form their opinion without knowing his feelings. B is wrong because they treat him as their daughters' "property." D is wrong because nothing suggests suspicion; the families eagerly regard him as a future husband for one of their daughters.

questions.passage: In Mark Twain's 1876 novel The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Tom is ordered to whitewash a long fence but convinces the other boys in town to pay him for the privilege of doing the work. The narrator presents Tom's success as revealing a general truth about what makes people want something, stating, ______blank
questions.question: Which quotation from The Adventures of Tom Sawyer most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: "He had discovered a great law of human action, without knowing it—namely, that in order to make a man or a boy covet a thing, it is only necessary to make the thing difficult to attain."
"He surveyed the fence, and all gladness left him and a deep melancholy settled down upon his spirit."
"Thirty yards of board fence nine feet high."
"If he hadn't run out of whitewash he would have bankrupted every boy in the village."
questions.correct_answer: "He had discovered a great law of human action, without knowing it—namely, that in order to make a man or a boy covet a thing, it is only necessary to make the thing difficult to attain."
questions.explanation: The claim is that the narrator presents Tom's success as revealing a general truth about what makes people want something. Choice A states such a truth: people "covet" what is "difficult to attain." B and C describe Tom's dismay at the chore before his scheme. D shows how successful the scheme was but offers no general truth about human desire.

questions.passage: In general, planets closer to the Sun have higher average surface temperatures because they receive more solar energy. But a planet's atmosphere can also strongly affect its temperature: Venus, for instance, has a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere that traps heat very effectively. A student claims that this heat-trapping effect can matter more than a planet's distance from the Sun, citing the example of ______blank
questions.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
options: Mars, which is the farthest from the Sun of the four planets and has the lowest mean surface temperature (−65°C).
Mercury, which is the closest of the four planets to the Sun (0.39 AU) and has a higher mean surface temperature (167°C) than Earth does (15°C).
Earth, whose mean surface temperature (15°C) is lower than that of Venus (464°C) but higher than that of Mars (−65°C).
Venus, which is nearly twice as far from the Sun as Mercury is (0.72 AU versus 0.39 AU) yet has a much higher mean surface temperature (464°C versus 167°C).
questions.correct_answer: Venus, which is nearly twice as far from the Sun as Mercury is (0.72 AU versus 0.39 AU) yet has a much higher mean surface temperature (464°C versus 167°C).
questions.explanation: The student claims an atmosphere's heat-trapping effect can matter more than distance from the Sun. Venus is farther from the Sun than Mercury but much hotter, so something other than distance, its atmosphere, must be responsible. A and B show the general pattern that closer planets are warmer, so they don't show atmosphere outweighing distance. C lists temperatures without connecting them to distance.

questions.passage: Dark roofs absorb sunlight and can intensify urban heat islands, areas of cities that are warmer than their surroundings. Engineer Priya Raman and colleagues compared the surface temperatures of three types of roofs in Phoenix, Arizona, on summer days. Vegetated roofs, which are covered with soil and plants, stay relatively cool as water evaporates from them, but their soil also stores heat and releases it slowly after sunset. The researchers concluded that for lowering roof surface temperatures, a white reflective coating outperformed vegetation at both times of day they measured, as shown by the fact that ______blank
questions.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
options: the dark asphalt roofs had higher average surface temperatures than both of the other roof types did at noon and at 9:00 p.m.
the white-coated roofs had lower average surface temperatures than the vegetated roofs did at both noon and 9:00 p.m.
the white-coated roofs averaged about 40°C at noon, compared with about 70°C for the dark asphalt roofs.
the vegetated roofs averaged about 45°C at noon but only about 30°C at 9:00 p.m.
questions.correct_answer: the white-coated roofs had lower average surface temperatures than the vegetated roofs did at both noon and 9:00 p.m.
questions.explanation: The conclusion is that a white coating did better than vegetation at both times of day. To support that, the data have to compare white-coated and vegetated roofs at noon and at 9:00 p.m. The graph shows white-coated roofs were cooler at both times (about 40°C versus 45°C at noon, and 25°C versus 30°C at 9:00 p.m.). A and C compare roofs with dark asphalt, not with each other. D describes only vegetated roofs.

questions.passage: Ice cores drilled from glaciers contain tiny bubbles of air that were trapped as snow was compressed into ice. Because the age of each layer of ice can be determined, scientists can analyze these bubbles to learn about the composition of Earth's atmosphere in the past. In regions where the surface of a glacier periodically melts and refreezes, however, meltwater can seep downward and alter older layers. Ice cores from such regions are therefore likely to ______blank
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: provide a less reliable record of past atmospheric composition than cores from regions where surface melting rarely occurs.
contain more trapped air bubbles than cores from regions where surface melting rarely occurs.
reveal that past atmospheres contained more water vapor than today's atmosphere does.
be more difficult to drill than cores from regions where surface melting rarely occurs.
questions.correct_answer: provide a less reliable record of past atmospheric composition than cores from regions where surface melting rarely occurs.
questions.explanation: Ice-core records are useful because each layer preserves air from a known time. If meltwater seeps down and alters older layers, the air in those layers no longer accurately reflects the time when they formed, so the record is less reliable. The text gives no basis for more bubbles (B), for conclusions about water vapor (C), or for drilling difficulty (D).

questions.passage: Astronomers often search for planets around other stars using the transit method, which detects the slight dimming of a star that occurs when a planet passes in front of it as seen from Earth. A transit can be observed only if a planet's orbit is aligned nearly edge-on from Earth's perspective. The chance of such an alignment depends on a planet's distance from its star: a planet orbiting very close to its star can be seen transiting across a much wider range of orbital orientations than can a planet orbiting far from its star. It follows that among the planets discovered by transit surveys, ______blank
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: planets orbiting far from their stars are likely easier to confirm than planets orbiting close to their stars are.
the proportion of planets with edge-on orbits is likely similar to the proportion of such planets among all planets orbiting the surveyed stars.
planets orbiting close to their stars are likely overrepresented relative to their actual share of all planets orbiting the surveyed stars.
planets orbiting close to their stars likely cause greater dimming during a transit than planets orbiting far from their stars do.
questions.correct_answer: planets orbiting close to their stars are likely overrepresented relative to their actual share of all planets orbiting the surveyed stars.
questions.explanation: Close-in planets can be seen transiting across a wider range of orbital orientations, so a transit survey is more likely to catch them than distant planets. The planets it finds will therefore include a larger share of close-in planets than actually exists. A isn't supported, since the text suggests distant planets are harder to detect. B is wrong because every planet detected by transit must have a nearly edge-on orbit. D isn't supported: the text discusses how likely a transit is to be observed, not how much a planet dims its star.

questions.passage: Launched in 1990, the Hubble Space Telescope ______blank images of galaxies so distant that the light it detects from them began traveling toward Earth billions of years ago.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun "the Hubble Space Telescope," so it needs the singular verb "has captured." "Have captured" is plural. "Capturing" and "to capture" aren't main verbs, so they would leave the sentence without one.

questions.passage: In 1869, geologist John Wesley Powell led an expedition down the Green and Colorado ______blank team became the first known group to travel the entire length of the Grand Canyon by boat.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: "In 1869 . . . Colorado Rivers" and "his team became . . . by boat" are both independent clauses, so a period correctly separates them. A creates a comma splice. B fuses the two clauses with no punctuation. D puts an unneeded comma after "and."

questions.passage: Engineers designing buildings for earthquake-prone regions sometimes place large bearings made of layered rubber and steel beneath a building's foundation. During an earthquake, these base isolators absorb much of the ground's motion, reducing the force that ______blank transmit to the structure above.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The pronoun refers to "these base isolators," a plural noun, so the plural pronoun "they" is correct. "It," "one," and "this" are singular.

questions.passage: Painter Georgia O'Keeffe is best known for her large, close-up paintings of ______blank also produced many landscapes depicting the deserts and mountains of northern New Mexico.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The sentence joins two independent clauses with the conjunctive adverb "however." A semicolon must come before "however" and a comma after it. B creates a comma splice, and C and D fail to separate the clauses correctly.

questions.passage: The Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, a nineteenth-century project that measured the subcontinent's landscape with remarkable precision and that eventually calculated the height of Mount Everest, ______blank teams of surveyors to haul heavy instruments across thousands of miles of difficult terrain.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The subject "The Great Trigonometrical Survey of India" is followed by a long appositive set off by commas, and the sentence still needs a main verb. "Required" is the only finite verb among the choices. "Requiring," "having required," and "to require" can't serve as the main verb, so they would leave the sentence incomplete.

questions.passage: Harriet Powers's Bible Quilt (1886)—which uses appliquéd figures to depict scenes such as Adam and Eve in the Garden of ______blank now held by the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History in Washington, DC.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The phrase beginning with "which uses" is extra information that opens with a dash after "(1886)." It has to close with a matching dash before the main verb "is." A comma (A) doesn't match the opening dash. A semicolon (B) can't separate a subject from its verb. No punctuation (C) leaves the dash unclosed.

questions.passage: Geysers form where groundwater is heated by hot rock deep underground. As the water heats, pressure builds until the water bursts through openings at the surface. ______blank Old Faithful in Yellowstone National Park erupts roughly every 60 to 110 minutes, shooting hot water more than 100 feet into the air.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The first two sentences explain in general how geysers erupt, and the last sentence describes one specific geyser, Old Faithful. "For example" signals that the sentence gives an instance of the general idea. There is no contrast (B or C), and the sentence doesn't summarize the text (D).

questions.passage: Early skyscrapers such as Chicago's Monadnock Building, completed in 1891, relied on thick masonry walls to support their weight; at the base of the building, the walls are about six feet thick. ______blank later skyscrapers used internal steel frames to carry their loads, which allowed their walls to be thin and their windows to be large.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The first sentence describes early skyscrapers that relied on thick masonry walls, and the second describes later skyscrapers that used steel frames and thin walls. "By contrast" signals this difference. "Similarly" signals likeness, "for instance" signals an example, and "as a result" suggests the thick walls caused the later design.

questions.passage: Carleton Watkins's large-format photographs of Yosemite Valley in the 1860s were admired for their technical brilliance, and they helped persuade members of Congress to protect the valley, which President Abraham Lincoln placed under the care of California in 1864. ______blank Watkins struggled financially for much of his career, and in the 1870s he lost his studio and many of his negatives to creditors.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The first sentence describes Watkins's admired and influential work, while the second says he struggled financially and lost his studio. "Even so" signals that the second point holds despite the first. "Consequently" wrongly suggests his success caused his troubles. "Likewise" signals similarity, and "in fact" signals that the second point reinforces the first.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Mount St. Helens is a volcano in Washington State.
  • It erupted on May 18, 1980.
  • The eruption was the deadliest volcanic event in US history.

questions.question: The student wants to state when Mount St. Helens erupted. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Mount St. Helens is a volcano located in Washington State.
The eruption of Mount St. Helens was the deadliest volcanic event in US history.
Mount St. Helens, a volcano in Washington State, erupted on May 18, 1980.
Fifty-seven people died when Mount St. Helens erupted.
questions.correct_answer: Mount St. Helens, a volcano in Washington State, erupted on May 18, 1980.
questions.explanation: The goal is to state when the eruption happened. Only C gives the date, May 18, 1980. A, B, and D give the volcano's location or the eruption's effects.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Europa is a moon of Jupiter.
  • Its surface is covered by a thick shell of ice.
  • Scientists believe an ocean of liquid water lies beneath the ice.
  • Europa is about 3,100 kilometers (km) in diameter.

  • Like Europa, Enceladus has an icy surface with an ocean of liquid water beneath it.

questions.question: The student wants to emphasize a difference in size between the two moons. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Enceladus, a moon of Saturn, is only about 500 kilometers in diameter, whereas Jupiter's moon Europa is about 3,100 kilometers across.
Like Europa, Enceladus has an icy surface with an ocean of liquid water beneath it.
Europa is a moon of Jupiter, and Enceladus is a moon of Saturn.
Europa, which is about 3,100 kilometers in diameter, is covered by a thick shell of ice.
questions.correct_answer: Enceladus, a moon of Saturn, is only about 500 kilometers in diameter, whereas Jupiter's moon Europa is about 3,100 kilometers across.
questions.explanation: Only A gives both moons' sizes and contrasts them with "whereas." B emphasizes a similarity, C gives the moons' planets, not their sizes, and D gives the size of only one moon.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Engineer Sofia Lindqvist and colleagues studied ways to reduce ice buildup on wind turbine blades.
  • Ice on blades reduces a turbine's efficiency and can break off dangerously.
  • The team tested a water-repelling coating on blades at a wind farm in northern Sweden.
  • They compared coated blades with uncoated blades over two winters.
  • Coated blades accumulated about 60% less ice than uncoated blades did.
questions.question: The student wants to present the study's findings to an audience already familiar with the problem of ice on wind turbine blades. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Ice on wind turbine blades reduces a turbine's efficiency and can break off dangerously, so Lindqvist and colleagues studied ways to reduce ice buildup.
Over two winters, blades with a water-repelling coating accumulated about 60% less ice than uncoated blades did, Lindqvist and colleagues found.
At a wind farm in northern Sweden, Lindqvist and colleagues compared blades that had a water-repelling coating with blades that did not.
Lindqvist and colleagues wanted to find out whether a water-repelling coating could reduce ice buildup on wind turbine blades.
questions.correct_answer: Over two winters, blades with a water-repelling coating accumulated about 60% less ice than uncoated blades did, Lindqvist and colleagues found.
questions.explanation: The goal is to present the findings. Because the audience already understands the problem, the sentence doesn't need to explain it. B states the result: coated blades collected about 60% less ice. A explains the problem and the study's purpose but gives no findings. C describes the method, and D describes the research question.

questions.passage: Honeybees communicate the location of food sources through a series of movements known as the waggle dance. By changing the angle and length of the dance, a returning forager can ______blank information about both the direction and the distance of flowers to the other bees in the hive.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The text says the dance's angle and length carry information about direction and distance to other bees, so the forager uses the dance to convey (communicate) that information. A is the opposite of sharing it; C and D don't describe passing information to other bees.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Willa Cather's 1913 novel O Pioneers!

One January day, thirty years ago, the little town of Hanover, anchored on a windy Nebraska tableland, was trying not to be blown away. A mist of fine snowflakes was curling and eddying about the cluster of low drab buildings huddled on the gray prairie, under a gray sky. The dwelling-houses were set about haphazard on the tough prairie sod; some of them looked as if they had been moved in overnight, and others as if they were straying off by themselves, headed straight for the open plain.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does the word “set” most nearly mean?
questions.explanation: The houses were “set about haphazard on the tough prairie sod,” and some looked as if they had been “moved in overnight”—that is, they were placed in scattered, random positions. “Set” doesn't mean hardened (as concrete sets), scheduled (as a date is set), or adjusted (as a clock is set) here.

questions.passage: In many parts of the Andes, farmers grow potatoes at altitudes where nighttime frost is common. Rather than viewing the cold nights as a problem, some communities have long ______blank them: potatoes are left outside to freeze overnight and then dried in the sun, producing chuño, a food that can be stored for years.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Instead of treating the freezing nights as a problem, communities use (exploit) them to freeze-dry potatoes into chuño, a food that keeps for years. “Feared” and “avoided” contradict “rather than viewing the cold nights as a problem”; “predicted” doesn't capture the practice of putting the cold to use.

questions.passage: When composer Elena Varga's piano études were first published, some critics dismissed them as ______blank, pointing to their short length and limited range of notes. Later performers, however, discovered that the pieces' apparent simplicity concealed intricate, shifting rhythms that challenged even highly skilled pianists.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Critics pointed to the pieces' short length and limited range of notes, and later performers found that their “apparent simplicity” hid complex rhythms. So the critics dismissed them as rudimentary (basic, simple). “Derivative” (unoriginal) isn't supported by the criticisms described; “contentious” (causing disagreement) and “extravagant” (excessive) conflict with the emphasis on simplicity.

questions.passage: The Atacama Desert in northern Chile is one of the driest places on Earth; some weather stations there have gone years without recording measurable rain. Yet life still finds a way to survive. Along the coast, a thick fog called camanchaca rolls in from the Pacific Ocean. Plants and lichens collect tiny droplets of water from the fog, and some local communities hang large mesh nets that capture fog water for drinking and farming.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe how living things and people obtain water in an extremely dry place
To compare the amount of rainfall in the Atacama Desert with that in other deserts
To argue that fog nets should replace wells as the main source of water in Chile
To explain why rain almost never falls in the Atacama Desert
questions.correct_answer: To describe how living things and people obtain water in an extremely dry place
questions.explanation: The text introduces the Atacama as extremely dry, then explains how plants, lichens, and communities get water from fog. B: no other deserts are compared. C: the text doesn't argue for replacing wells. D: the text notes the lack of rain but doesn't explain its cause.

questions.passage: Marathon runners often slow down in the final miles of a race, a pattern many coaches attribute simply to fatigue. Sports scientist Tomás Lindqvist and colleagues wondered whether decisions made early in a race might also play a role. They analyzed split times from more than 10,000 runners and found that those who started fastest relative to their eventual average pace were the most likely to slow dramatically near the finish. The researchers suggest that a more even early pace may help runners avoid late-race slowdowns.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It introduces a hypothesis that the researchers later reject.
It describes a common explanation for late-race slowdowns that the researchers accept without question.
It presents the finding on which the researchers base their suggestion about pacing.
It notes a limitation of the method the researchers used to collect their data.
questions.correct_answer: It presents the finding on which the researchers base their suggestion about pacing.
questions.explanation: The underlined sentence reports what the researchers found (fast starters slowed the most), and the next sentence builds on that finding to suggest a more even early pace. A: no hypothesis is rejected. B: the common explanation (fatigue) appears in the first sentence, and the researchers look beyond it. D: no limitation is mentioned.

By noting that high energy costs currently limit vertical farms mainly to a narrow range of crops
By arguing that vertical farms actually require more land than conventional farms do
By suggesting that produce from vertical farms reaches shoppers more slowly than supporters claim
questions.correct_answer: By noting that high energy costs currently limit vertical farms mainly to a narrow range of crops
questions.explanation: Text 2 grants that vertical farms have advantages but says electricity costs make them profitable mainly for lettuce and herbs, not the staple crops that supply most calories—so it would qualify the claim of a worldwide transformation. A contradicts Text 2's point about staple crops. C and D aren't claims Text 2 makes.

questions.passage: The didgeridoo is a wind instrument traditionally made by Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia. questions.question: Which choice best states the main topic of the text?
options: The diet of termites in northern Australia
Painting styles used by artists in Australia
How the didgeridoo is made and played
questions.correct_answer: How the didgeridoo is made and played
questions.explanation: Every sentence concerns the didgeridoo: the branches it's made from, how it's shaped and decorated, and how it's played. Termites (A) and painted designs (B) are details of that process, and orchestras (C) aren't mentioned.

questions.passage: Emperor penguins breed during the harsh Antarctic winter. After a female lays a single egg, she carefully passes it to her mate, who balances it on his feet and covers it with a warm fold of skin called a brood pouch. The females then travel to the sea to feed, while the males huddle together against the wind for about two months, eating nothing, until the eggs hatch.
questions.question: According to the text, what do male emperor penguins do while the females are at sea?
options: They gather stones to build nests for the eggs.
They take turns traveling to the sea to catch fish.
They keep the eggs warm while going without food.
They teach the newly hatched chicks to swim.
questions.correct_answer: They keep the eggs warm while going without food.
questions.explanation: The text says each male balances the egg on his feet under a brood pouch and that the males huddle for about two months “eating nothing” until the eggs hatch. Nests (A), fishing trips (B), and swimming lessons (D) aren't mentioned.

questions.passage: For decades, many historians of West African music assumed that the kora, a 21-string harp-lute associated with the Mandinka people, had changed little since the instrument first emerged. However, ethnomusicologist Awa Keita's review of recordings made over the course of the twentieth century shows that kora players continually adjusted their tunings, borrowed techniques from guitar music, and developed new solo repertoires. Keita argues that the kora tradition is best understood not as a fixed inheritance but as an ongoing practice shaped by each generation of players.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Kora players in the twentieth century largely abandoned traditional tunings and techniques in favor of those used in guitar music.
Evidence from twentieth-century recordings suggests that the kora tradition has been continually reshaped by its players rather than remaining unchanged.
Historical recordings of kora music are too limited to reveal how the instrument's tradition has developed over time.
The kora most likely emerged more recently than many historians of West African music had assumed.
questions.correct_answer: Evidence from twentieth-century recordings suggests that the kora tradition has been continually reshaped by its players rather than remaining unchanged.
questions.explanation: The text contrasts an older assumption (the kora changed little) with Keita's findings (players kept adapting tunings, techniques, and repertoire) and her conclusion that the tradition is “an ongoing practice shaped by each generation.” A overstates: borrowing some guitar techniques isn't abandoning tradition. C contradicts the text, which uses recordings as evidence. D: the text doesn't discuss when the kora emerged.

questions.passage: In several songbird species, individuals that live in cities sing at a higher pitch than members of the same species that live in forests. Ecologist Hana Morita hypothesizes that city birds raise the pitch of their songs so that the songs are not drowned out by traffic noise, which is concentrated at low frequencies.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Morita's hypothesis?
options: City birds of these species sing at a higher pitch on weekdays, when traffic is heavy, than on weekends, when traffic is light.
Forest birds of these species sing more often in the early morning than at any other time of day.
City birds of these species tend to have slightly larger bodies than forest birds of the same species.
City birds of these species that live in quiet parks sing at the same pitch as those that live near busy roads.
questions.correct_answer: City birds of these species sing at a higher pitch on weekdays, when traffic is heavy, than on weekends, when traffic is light.
questions.explanation: If pitch rises when traffic noise rises and falls when it falls, that links higher pitch directly to traffic noise, supporting the hypothesis. B concerns forest birds' timing, not pitch or noise. C is unrelated to noise. D would weaken the hypothesis, since pitch wouldn't vary with traffic.

questions.passage: In many dry farming regions, water for irrigation is increasingly scarce. Agronomist Priya Natarajan compared three irrigation methods in a season-long trial with tomato plants, measuring how much water each method applied and how much fruit the plants produced. Natarajan concluded that drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to plant roots through small tubes, can reduce water use without lowering yields compared with the other methods tested.
questions.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Natarajan's conclusion?
options: Furrow irrigation applied 260 liters of water per plant, the most of any method.
Plants irrigated with sprinklers had an average yield of 4.4 kilograms per plant.
Sprinkler-irrigated plants had a higher average yield than furrow-irrigated plants did.
Drip irrigation applied less water per plant than either other method did, and drip-irrigated plants had the highest average yield.
questions.correct_answer: Drip irrigation applied less water per plant than either other method did, and drip-irrigated plants had the highest average yield.
questions.explanation: The conclusion has two parts: drip irrigation uses less water, and yields aren't lower. D addresses both (120 liters, the least; 4.6 kg, the highest). A, B, and C are accurate but don't involve drip irrigation at all.

questions.passage: Many athletes stretch before exercising, but some sports scientists question whether static stretching—holding a stretch in place for 30 seconds or more—is the best preparation for activities that require speed. Sports scientist Daniel Okafor had soccer players and basketball players run a 30-meter sprint after each of three warm-up routines, completed on different days: no warm-up, static stretching, and a dynamic warm-up made up of movements such as leg swings and skips. Okafor concluded that the dynamic warm-up was the most effective preparation for sprinting for both groups of athletes.
questions.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Okafor's conclusion?
options: Soccer players had faster average sprint times than basketball players did after each of the three warm-up routines.
For both soccer players and basketball players, the average sprint time was lowest after the dynamic warm-up.
Basketball players' average sprint time after static stretching was about 4.75 seconds.
Soccer players' average sprint time was higher after static stretching than after no warm-up.
questions.correct_answer: For both soccer players and basketball players, the average sprint time was lowest after the dynamic warm-up.
questions.explanation: A lower sprint time means a faster sprint. Okafor's conclusion is that the dynamic warm-up worked best for both groups, and B shows exactly that: soccer players' lowest time (4.48 s) and basketball players' lowest time (4.55 s) both came after the dynamic warm-up. A compares the two groups rather than the routines. C gives a single value. D compares only static stretching and no warm-up for one group.

questions.passage: Koalas eat almost nothing but eucalyptus leaves, which are low in nutrients and contain compounds that are toxic to many animals. A koala's long caecum, a pouch in its digestive system, contains microbes that help break down these compounds. Young koalas aren't born with the microbes, however. Instead, they get them by eating pap, a substance produced by their mothers. Therefore, a young koala that did not eat pap would most likely ______blank
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: prefer eucalyptus leaves to other foods.
develop a longer caecum than other koalas do.
produce pap for its own offspring earlier than other koalas do.
questions.explanation: Koalas need caecum microbes to break down eucalyptus compounds, and young koalas get those microbes only by eating pap. A young koala that didn't eat pap would lack the microbes and so would struggle to digest eucalyptus. B, C, and D aren't connected to the missing microbes.

questions.passage: Some farmers plant strips of flowering plants alongside crop fields to attract ladybugs and other insects that eat crop pests. Agricultural ecologist Rafael Ortega compared cabbage fields with and without such flower strips and found fewer aphids, a common cabbage pest, in fields with the strips. However, the effect was strongest in parts of fields within 50 meters of the strips and was barely detectable in parts more than 100 meters away. These results suggest that ______blank
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: ladybugs are attracted more strongly to cabbage plants than to flowering plants.
flower strips increase the number of aphids in parts of fields that are far from the strips.
aphids are not a significant source of food for ladybugs and similar insects.
farmers with large fields may need to plant flower strips within their fields, not only along the edges, to reduce aphids throughout the fields.
questions.correct_answer: farmers with large fields may need to plant flower strips within their fields, not only along the edges, to reduce aphids throughout the fields.
questions.explanation: The benefit of flower strips was strong within 50 meters and barely detectable beyond 100 meters, so in a large field, strips only at the edge would leave distant areas unprotected; placing strips within the field would address that. A isn't supported by any comparison in the text. B contradicts the finding (the effect faded; aphids didn't increase). C contradicts the premise that ladybugs eat aphids.

questions.passage: Found in the rainforests of Sumatra and Borneo, the parasitic plant Rafflesia arnoldii produces the largest individual flower of any known plant. The flower can measure up to one meter ______blank it has no leaves, stems, or roots of its own.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: Both “The flower can measure up to one meter across” and “it has no leaves, stems, or roots of its own” are independent clauses, and a semicolon correctly joins them. A creates a comma splice, B a run-on sentence, and D an ungrammatical relative clause (“which it has no leaves”).

questions.passage: Sea otters are among the few mammals known to use tools. When a sea otter finds a clam or sea urchin, it often floats on ______blank back and cracks the shell open against a rock balanced on its chest.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The pronoun refers to “a sea otter,” which is singular, and the sentence needs a possessive (the otter's back), so “its” is correct. B and D are plural; C and D are contractions (“it is,” “they are”), not possessives.

questions.passage: ______blank style of throat singing practiced in Mongolia and the Russian republic of Tuva, allows a single performer to produce two or more distinct pitches at the same time.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: “A style of throat singing practiced in Mongolia and the Russian republic of Tuva” is a nonessential appositive describing khoomei. It is already closed by a comma after “Tuva,” so it must be opened with a matching comma. A omits the opening comma; a semicolon (C) or colon (D) can't separate a subject from the rest of its clause.

questions.passage: The spices used in berbere, an Ethiopian seasoning blend that often includes chili peppers, fenugreek, and ginger, ______blank from region to region and even from family to family.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The subject of the verb is the plural noun “spices,” not the singular “blend” inside the appositive, so the plural verb “vary” is needed. A, B, and D are singular verbs.

questions.passage: Along the Silk Road, goods and ideas passed through a series of major trading cities, including Chang'an (present-day Xi'an), ______blank Samarkand, Uzbekistan; and Baghdad, Iraq.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The sentence lists cities whose names already contain commas (“Samarkand, Uzbekistan”), so the items must be separated by semicolons, matching the semicolon after “Uzbekistan.” A comma (A) or no punctuation (C) blurs where one item ends; a colon (B) can't separate list items.

questions.passage: The seed vault on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen, built deep inside a mountain to protect more than one million samples of crop seeds from around the world, ______blank as a backup in case seeds stored elsewhere are lost to war or natural disasters.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The sentence's subject is “The seed vault,” which needs a main verb; the long participial phrase beginning “built deep inside a mountain” only describes it. The singular finite verb “serves” agrees with “vault.” A and D are nonfinite forms that leave the sentence without a main verb; C is plural, agreeing wrongly with “seeds” or “samples.”

questions.passage: The durian, a fruit grown in Southeast Asia, is famous for its strong smell. Many people find the odor unpleasant, and some hotels and public transit systems in Singapore have banned the fruit. ______blank many others consider durian a delicacy and call it the “king of fruits.”
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The previous sentences describe people who dislike durian's smell (and bans on the fruit); this sentence describes people who love it. “However” signals that contrast. A and D suggest the sentence continues the same idea, and B suggests it results from the bans.

questions.passage: Salmon hatch in freshwater streams and then migrate to the ocean, where they spend several years feeding and growing. ______blank they return to the very streams where they hatched to lay their own eggs.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The text follows the salmon's life in order: hatching, migrating to the ocean, spending several years there, and then returning to spawn. “Eventually” marks this later stage after a long period. A treats the sentence as an example, B as a replacement for what came before, and C as a similar action.

questions.passage: Scott Joplin's opera Treemonisha, published in 1911, was never fully staged during his lifetime. In 1915 Joplin presented a read-through of the work with no scenery, costumes, or orchestra, accompanying the singers himself on the piano, but it attracted little notice before his death in 1917. ______blank the opera eventually received its first full production in 1972, and in 1976 Joplin was posthumously awarded a special Pulitzer Prize for his contributions to American music.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: During Joplin's lifetime, Treemonisha was never fully staged, and its one read-through attracted little notice; later, it received a full production and Joplin received a special Pulitzer Prize. “Still” signals this later recognition despite the earlier disappointment. B wrongly presents the later success as caused by the neglect; C and D present it as similar to or a restatement of the neglect.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The dhol is a double-headed drum.
  • It is widely played in Punjab, a region of India and Pakistan.
  • It is often played at weddings and harvest festivals.
questions.question: The student wants to identify where the dhol is widely played. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The dhol is a double-headed drum that is often played at weddings.
The dhol is widely played in Punjab, a region of India and Pakistan.
Drums like the dhol are sometimes played at harvest festivals.
The dhol has two drumheads, one on each end.
questions.correct_answer: The dhol is widely played in Punjab, a region of India and Pakistan.
questions.explanation: Only B states where the dhol is widely played (Punjab). A and C describe occasions when it is played, and D describes its construction.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Sea turtles lay their eggs in nests on sandy beaches.
  • The temperature of the sand affects whether hatchlings develop as male or female.
  • Warmer nests (above about 29°C, or 84°F) produce mostly females.
  • Cooler nests produce mostly males.
  • Rising beach temperatures could lead to populations with far more females than males.
questions.question: The student wants to explain how nest temperature affects sea turtle hatchlings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Sea turtles lay their eggs in nests that they dig on sandy beaches.
Rising beach temperatures could lead to sea turtle populations with far more females than males.
The temperature of the sand is one of several factors that affect sea turtle nests.
Sea turtle nests in warmer sand produce mostly female hatchlings, while nests in cooler sand produce mostly males.
questions.correct_answer: Sea turtle nests in warmer sand produce mostly female hatchlings, while nests in cooler sand produce mostly males.
questions.explanation: D explains the effect of temperature on hatchlings: warm nests produce mostly females and cool nests mostly males. A doesn't mention temperature. B describes a possible future consequence rather than the effect itself. C is vague and adds a claim (“several factors”) not in the notes.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The Sahara, in northern Africa, is the world's largest hot desert.
  • It covers about 9 million square kilometers.
  • Much of the Sahara receives less than 100 millimeters of rain per year.
  • The Gobi Desert, in China and Mongolia, covers about 1.3 million square kilometers.
  • The Gobi is a cold desert; winter temperatures can drop below −30°C.
questions.question: The student wants to emphasize a difference in size between the two deserts. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The Sahara and the Gobi are both deserts, but the Gobi is located in China and Mongolia.
The Gobi is a cold desert where winter temperatures can drop below −30°C.
At about 9 million square kilometers, the Sahara is roughly seven times as large as the Gobi, which covers about 1.3 million square kilometers.
Much of the Sahara, the world's largest hot desert, receives less than 100 millimeters of rain per year.
questions.correct_answer: At about 9 million square kilometers, the Sahara is roughly seven times as large as the Gobi, which covers about 1.3 million square kilometers.
questions.explanation: C compares the areas of both deserts (about 9 million vs. about 1.3 million square kilometers), directly emphasizing the size difference. A contrasts location, B and D each describe only one desert's climate.

questions.passage: In linguistics, a calque is a word or phrase borrowed from another language through literal, word-for-word translation rather than through adoption of the original sounds. The English term "flea market," for instance, is ______blank the French expression marché aux puces, whose components translate directly as "market of the fleas."
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The text defines a calque as a borrowing made through literal, word-for-word translation, and it notes that the parts of the French phrase translate directly as "market of the fleas." "Flea market" is therefore modeled on the French phrase. It is not antithetical to (opposed to) it, and it is not indistinguishable from it, since the words themselves are English. Nothing suggests that the English term superseded (replaced) the French one.

questions.passage: Historian Leena Marwah contends that the account books kept by eighteenth-century Gujarati merchant houses are far from dry records of transactions: their marginal annotations about monsoon winds, rumors of war, and the trustworthiness of distant agents ______blank an acute awareness of the risks inherent in long-distance trade.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The text says the ledgers are "far from dry records": their notes on weather, rumors of war, and unreliable agents show the merchants' awareness of risk. "Evince" means to reveal or show clearly, so it fits. "Belie" means to contradict or give a false impression of, which is the opposite of what the text describes. Annotations can't "forestall" (prevent) or "mitigate" (lessen) an awareness. They can only record it.

questions.passage: In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, copyists and restorers working on the Buddhist cave murals at Ajanta, India, coated several of the faded paintings with varnish and shellac, hoping to brighten and protect them. Rather than restoring the images, however, the coatings yellowed, darkened, and cracked over the following decades, partially ______blank the very details they had been intended to preserve.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The coatings were meant to brighten and protect the murals, but they "darkened and cracked," which worked against the goal of preserving the details. "Obscuring" (hiding, making hard to see) fits this contrast. "Accentuating" (emphasizing) and "reconstituting" (rebuilding) describe the results the conservators hoped for, not what happened. "Corroborating" (confirming) does not make sense when describing the effect of a coating on painted details.

questions.passage: Economist Priya Venkataraman argues that the apparent stability of the country's currency during the 1990s was ______blank: official exchange rates held steady only because the central bank quietly drew down its foreign reserves, a practice that could not be sustained and that ended in an abrupt devaluation in 1999.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The text explains that the exchange rate "held steady only because" the central bank secretly used up its reserves, and that this ended in a sudden devaluation. So the stability was only apparent, not real. "Illusory" means exactly that. "Inevitable" doesn't fit a stability that couldn't last. "Unprecedented" (never seen before) and "contentious" (disputed) are not supported: the text says nothing about precedent or debate.

questions.passage: Glass is often described as a liquid that flows extremely slowly, a claim commonly supported by the observation that windowpanes in old European churches are thicker at the bottom than at the top. Yet panes of similar age are sometimes found installed with their thicker edges at the top or sides. Materials scientists attribute the uneven thickness to the way the glass was made: older techniques produced sheets of irregular thickness, and glaziers often set the heavier edge at the bottom for stability. Calculations further indicate that at room temperature, noticeable flow in such glass would take far longer than the age of the universe.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It presents an observation that undermines a piece of evidence offered in support of a popular claim.
It offers an explanation of how medieval glassmakers produced sheets of uneven thickness.
It identifies a question about old windowpanes that materials scientists have been unable to answer.
It provides additional support for the idea that glass flows noticeably at room temperature.
questions.correct_answer: It presents an observation that undermines a piece of evidence offered in support of a popular claim.
questions.explanation: The popular claim is that glass flows, and the evidence given for it is that old panes are thicker at the bottom. The underlined sentence notes that some panes of the same age have their thick edges at the top or sides, which gravity-driven flow can't explain. It undermines that evidence. The explanation of how the glass was made comes in the next sentence (B). The text answers the question rather than leaving it open (C), and the sentence weakens the flow idea instead of supporting it (D).

questions.passage: Linguists have long assumed that languages spoken in isolated communities change more slowly than languages in frequent contact with their neighbors, since contact introduces loanwords and new grammatical patterns. Analyzing records of 81 Austronesian languages, linguist Rafael Ocampo and colleagues found the opposite tendency for vocabulary: languages spoken on remote islands replaced core words, such as those for body parts and numbers, at higher rates than did languages on well-connected islands. Ocampo proposes that in small, isolated populations, a new word introduced by a few speakers is less likely to be outweighed by the many speakers who retain older forms, allowing innovations to spread more quickly.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a method for reconstructing the vocabularies of ancient languages, identifies a flaw in that method, and proposes a way to correct it.
It outlines two competing hypotheses about language change, presents evidence supporting each, and argues that neither is complete.
It presents a widely held assumption, reports a finding that runs counter to that assumption, and offers a possible explanation for the finding.
It explains how contact between communities introduces new words, gives an example from Austronesian languages, and predicts how those languages will change.
questions.correct_answer: It presents a widely held assumption, reports a finding that runs counter to that assumption, and offers a possible explanation for the finding.
questions.explanation: The text opens with what linguists "have long assumed" (isolated languages change more slowly). Next it reports Ocampo's finding of "the opposite tendency" for vocabulary. It ends with Ocampo's proposed explanation involving small populations. No method is critiqued (A), and only one hypothesis is evaluated (B). The text doesn't predict future change, and contact appears only as part of the assumption being challenged (D).

questions.passage:
Text 1

Economists have often explained the rapid spread of mobile money services in Kenya in the late 2000s chiefly as a triumph of technology: inexpensive phones and a simple text-message interface let millions of people without bank accounts send and receive payments. In his history of the service's rollout, economist Daniel Mwangi goes further, arguing that the service's success was all but guaranteed once mobile phones became affordable to most Kenyan households.

Text 2

According to economist Grace Achieng, technology alone cannot account for mobile money's success in Kenya: similar services launched in other countries with comparably cheap phones attracted few users. What distinguished the Kenyan case, Achieng argues, was a dense network of small shops that served as agents where customers could convert cash into digital credit and back again, a network built by recruiting shopkeepers who were already trusted in their neighborhoods.
questions.question: Based on the texts, how would Achieng (Text 2) most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?
options: By arguing that economists have overstated how affordable mobile phones were in Kenya in the late 2000s
By agreeing that technology was decisive but noting that the text-message interface mattered more than the price of phones
By claiming that fewer Kenyans lacked bank accounts at the time than Mwangi's account assumes
By pointing out that affordable phones did not lead to comparable success in other countries, which suggests that another factor was essential
questions.correct_answer: By pointing out that affordable phones did not lead to comparable success in other countries, which suggests that another factor was essential
questions.explanation: Text 1's underlined claim is that success was "all but guaranteed" once phones became cheap. Text 2 says similar services in countries with "comparably cheap phones attracted few users." Achieng credits Kenya's network of trusted shopkeeper agents instead. She would therefore say cheap phones weren't enough. Text 2 never questions the phones' affordability (A) or the number of unbanked people (C). It explicitly rejects the idea that technology was decisive (B).

questions.passage: Most rechargeable batteries in electronic devices rely on lithium, whose extraction consumes large quantities of water and is concentrated in a few countries. Sodium, by contrast, is abundant in seawater and rock salt, and sodium-ion batteries operate on similar chemical principles. The sodium ion is considerably larger than the lithium ion, however, so it moves less easily through many electrode materials developed for lithium batteries and can strain and crack them during repeated charging. Consequently, much current research on sodium-ion batteries concentrates less on their basic chemistry than on designing electrode structures with channels spacious enough to accommodate sodium ions.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Although sodium-ion batteries offer an advantage related to the abundance of sodium, the size of sodium ions has led researchers to focus on developing suitable electrode materials.
Sodium-ion batteries are likely to replace lithium-ion batteries once engineers develop electrodes that do not crack during charging.
Because sodium ions are larger than lithium ions, sodium-ion batteries store more energy than lithium-ion batteries do but charge more slowly.
Researchers have largely abandoned efforts to understand the chemistry of sodium-ion batteries in favor of finding new sources of lithium.
questions.correct_answer: Although sodium-ion batteries offer an advantage related to the abundance of sodium, the size of sodium ions has led researchers to focus on developing suitable electrode materials.
questions.explanation: The text sets sodium's abundance against lithium's limited supply. It then explains that the larger sodium ion strains electrodes built for lithium, which is why research now focuses on electrode structures. Choice A covers both points. The text makes no prediction that sodium-ion batteries will replace lithium-ion ones (B), says nothing about energy storage or charging speed (C), and doesn't mention a search for new lithium sources (D).

questions.passage: In many societies, gifts create obligations: a recipient is expected eventually to reciprocate, and a gift left unreturned can mark the recipient as socially subordinate to the giver. Studying exchange networks in highland villages in Papua New Guinea, anthropologist Samuel Kerowa observed that residents sometimes deliberately delayed returning gifts for years, even when they could easily afford to reciprocate. Kerowa argues that the delay was itself meaningful: an outstanding debt kept the relationship between two households active, whereas prompt repayment could signal a wish to settle accounts and bring the relationship to a close.
questions.question: Based on the text, why does Kerowa believe some residents delayed returning gifts?
options: They lacked the resources to reciprocate promptly and waited until they could afford a gift of equal value.
They wished to demonstrate their social superiority over the households that had given them gifts.
Leaving a debt outstanding helped keep an ongoing relationship with the giver's household active.
They regarded prompt repayment as an insult because it implied that the original gift had been inadequate.
questions.correct_answer: Leaving a debt outstanding helped keep an ongoing relationship with the giver's household active.
questions.explanation: The text says Kerowa believes the delay was meaningful: "an outstanding debt kept the relationship between two households active," while quick repayment could signal a wish to end it. The residents delayed "even when they could easily afford to reciprocate," which rules out A. The text says an unreturned gift can mark the recipient as subordinate, the opposite of B. Choice D's claim that prompt repayment was an insult is never made.

questions.passage: Literary scholar Hana Okafor argues that the frequent digressions in Laurence Sterne's novel Tristram Shandy (1759-1767) should not be read as failures of narrative discipline. Sterne's narrator repeatedly interrupts the story of his own life to comment on minor characters, on philosophy, and on the difficulty of writing itself, so that well into the third volume he has barely reached the moment of his own birth. For Okafor, these interruptions are the novel's true subject: by showing that any life story could be extended indefinitely by the associations each event suggests, Sterne questions whether a life can be narrated in an orderly sequence at all.
questions.question: Which statement about Okafor's interpretation of Tristram Shandy is best supported by the text?
options: Okafor suggests that Sterne intended the digressions to be skipped by readers interested mainly in the narrator's life.
Okafor maintains that the digressions show that Sterne was more interested in philosophy than in the events of his narrator's life.
Okafor argues that Sterne abandoned his original plan for the novel after its early volumes grew too long.
Okafor believes that the novel's seemingly undisciplined form is central to a point it makes about the difficulty of telling a life story from beginning to end.
questions.correct_answer: Okafor believes that the novel's seemingly undisciplined form is central to a point it makes about the difficulty of telling a life story from beginning to end.
questions.explanation: For Okafor, the digressions are "the novel's true subject." By showing that any life story could be stretched out without end, Sterne "questions whether a life can be narrated in an orderly sequence at all." So the digressive form is central to a point about the difficulty of telling a life story in sequence (D). Choice A treats the digressions as unimportant, which contradicts Okafor's view. Philosophy is only one of several digression topics, and Okafor's point concerns narration, not a preference for philosophy (B). Nothing in the text concerns Sterne abandoning a plan (C).

questions.passage: Sickle blades (small flint tools set into wooden or bone handles) found at many Neolithic sites in Southwest Asia often bear a distinctive glossy polish along their cutting edges. At one such site, where the blades were frequently recovered near storage pits containing charred grain, archaeologist Yael Barak hypothesizes that the polish formed as a result of repeatedly harvesting cereal stalks, which contain abrasive particles of silica, and therefore indicates that the blades were used primarily for cereal harvesting.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Barak's hypothesis?
options: Charred grain recovered from the storage pits at the site came from both wild and domesticated cereal species.
Flint blades used experimentally to cut only reeds and sedges, which also contain silica, developed a polish indistinguishable under a microscope from that on the Neolithic blades.
Some sickle blades from the site show polish on both edges, suggesting that they were removed from their handles and reset.
The polish on blades from the site is more extensive than the polish on blades from older sites nearby.
questions.correct_answer: Flint blades used experimentally to cut only reeds and sedges, which also contain silica, developed a polish indistinguishable under a microscope from that on the Neolithic blades.
questions.explanation: Barak concludes from the polish that the blades were used to harvest cereals. If cutting reeds and sedges produces exactly the same polish, the polish can't show that the blades were used on cereals, which weakens the hypothesis. Choice A is still consistent with cereal harvesting, since wild cereals are cereals too. Reset blades (C) and more extensive polish (D) say nothing about which plants were cut.

questions.passage: Potters in many societies mix temper (added material such as crushed rock, called grit; burned and crushed shell; or plant fiber) into clay to keep vessels from cracking as they dry and are fired. At a site in the Mississippi River valley, archaeologist Adaeze Nwosu classified pottery sherds (fragments) from four excavation layers by temper type; Layer 4 is the deepest and oldest, and Layer 1 is the uppermost and most recent. Nwosu concluded that at this site, shell tempering displaced grit tempering gradually over several centuries rather than replacing it abruptly.
questions.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Nwosu's conclusion?
options: The total number of sherds recovered was greater in Layer 1 than in Layer 4, and fiber-tempered sherds made up a smaller percentage of the sherds in Layer 1 than in Layer 4.
Shell-tempered sherds made up 79% of the sherds in Layer 1 but only 4% of the sherds in Layer 4.
Grit-tempered sherds made up a larger percentage of the sherds than shell-tempered sherds did in Layer 3 but not in Layer 2.

The percentage of shell-tempered sherds increased in each successive layer from Layer 4 to Layer 1 (from 4% to 27% to 52% to 79%), while the percentage of grit-tempered sherds decreased in each successive layer.
questions.correct_answer: The percentage of shell-tempered sherds increased in each successive layer from Layer 4 to Layer 1 (from 4% to 27% to 52% to 79%), while the percentage of grit-tempered sherds decreased in each successive layer.
questions.explanation: To show that shell tempering took over gradually rather than abruptly, the data must show a steady change across the layers. Choice D shows shell tempering rising and grit tempering falling in every successive layer. Choice B compares only the first and last layers, which would also fit a sudden switch. Choice C describes a single crossover point, and choice A concerns total sherd counts and fiber tempering, which are irrelevant to the conclusion.

questions.passage: Apprenticeship programs combine paid work with structured job training, but economists disagree about whether their benefits last. Economist Ingrid Solberg tracked the median weekly earnings of three groups of construction-trade workers: those who completed an apprenticeship, those who entered an apprenticeship but left before completing it, and a comparison group of workers with similar backgrounds who never entered one. Solberg concluded that the earnings advantage associated with completing an apprenticeship is not merely a short-lived boost from earning a credential but instead grows as workers' careers progress.
questions.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Solberg's conclusion?
